item.title: Le Pentagone veut diffuser en direct l'exécution de l'auteur de la fusillade de Ford Hood
item.description: Le Pentagone a annoncé son intention de diffuser en direct l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, qui avait tué 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ce qui serait sans précédent aux Etats-Unis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le Pentagone a annoncé son intention de diffuser en direct l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, qui avait tué 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ce qui serait sans précédent aux Etats-Unis. Nidal Hasan, un ancien psychiatre de l'armée de terre condamné à mort en 2013 par un tribunal militaire, doit être fusillé par un peloton d'exécution le 3 décembre. Le secrétaire à la Défense, Pete Hegseth, a particulièrement poussé en faveur de cette décision. "Nous ferons en sorte que les gens puissent la regarder, qu'elle soit publique, car les gens doivent comprendre que ce genre de choses a de graves conséquences", a dit Pete Hegseth. Le président Donald Trump est pour l'heure resté silencieux. Interrogé à ce sujet, le vice-président J.D. Vance a dit ignorer si l'exécution serait bel et bien diffusée. "Si cest le cas, je ne regarderai pas", a-t-il déclaré. Certains élus républicains et stratèges conservateurs ont critiqué cette décision. Le sénateur républicain de Caroline du Nord, Thom Tillis, a qualifié l'idée de "plus que répugnante" dans un message sur les réseaux sociaux. "Les exécutions publiques sont le propre de dictatures oppressives comme l'Iran et l'Afghanistan", a déclaré le sénateur, qui s'oppose fréquemment à Donald Trump et ne briguera pas un nouveau mandat aux élections de mi-mandat début novembre. "Cela ne devrait pas arriver en Amérique", a-t-il insisté. L'autorité fédérale des télécommunications, la FCC, n'a pas pris position sur la question de savoir si les réseaux américains pourraient diffuser une telle exécution. Un rapport de 2007 de la FCC sur la violence à la télévision indiquait que l'agence n'avait pas le pouvoir de réglementer les contenus violents. Le rapport précisait que, selon la jurisprudence des tribunaux, "les discours violents et les représentations de la violence sont protégés par le premier amendement" de la Constitution américaine garantissant la liberté d'expression. L'armée américaine n'a pas eu recours au peloton d'exécution pour un condamné à mort depuis 1945, peu après la fin de la Seconde Guerre mondiale. Nidal Hasan avait ouvert le feu dans un secteur de la base de Fort Hood où des soldats passaient des tests d'évaluation avant d'être envoyés en Irak ou en Afghanistan, et a déclaré à des psychiatres après son arrestation qu'il voulait devenir un martyr. Il a été reconnu coupable de 13 chefs de meurtre avec préméditation et de 32 autres de tentative de meurtre avec préméditation à l'issue de son procès en 2013 et condamné à mort. La dernière exécution d'un militaire d'active par l'armée américaine remonte à 1961.

item.title: US announces effort to disrupt hacking infrastructure run by China's Integrity Tech Group
item.description: The United States said it is seizing seven internet domains to disrupt hackers it accuses of working with Chinese IT firm Integrity Technology Group.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: The United States said it is seizing seven internet domains to disrupt hackers it accuses of working with Chinese IT firm Integrity Technology Group. The Justice Department said in a statement issued on Thursday that the domains were being used to help Chinese hackers scan and hack US and foreign critical infrastructure systems. Integrity Tech did not respond to a request for comment. The Justice Department said the move was the second public effort to disrupt Integrity Tech’s hacking infrastructure. In September 2024, the department announced the [USN:W1N3FL03H TEXT:"court-authorized disruption"] of an Integrity Tech botnet consisting of more than 250,000 compromised consumer devices in the US and across the world. At the time, then-FBI Director Christopher Wray said that Integrity Tech was behind a major Chinese hacking group nicknamed "Flax Typhoon" and was carrying out intelligence collection and reconnaissance functions for Beijing's security agencies. The Chinese Embassy in Washington said in a statement on Thursday that it "firmly opposes and combats hacking activities in accordance with law. China also firmly opposes spreading disinformation and making noises for political agenda."

item.title: Oil falls as Trump comments on Iran talks ease supply fears
item.description: Oil prices fell on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before midterm elections next month and talked of "productive" talks to end their war that has disrupted global energy markets.
item.dc:creator: Erwin Seba
item.content:encoded: Oil prices fell on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before midterm elections next month and talked of "productive" talks to end their war that has disrupted global energy markets. Trump also teased an upcoming, undisclosed announcement on diesel and said he was considering suspending the federal gasoline tax. Brent crude futures slid 52 cents, 0.50% on Friday to $103.76 a barrel by 12:11 a.m. CDT (1811 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 22 cents or 0.2% to $91.28. Plans by China, the world's top oil importer, to [USN:L1N45V02I TEXT:"resume refined fuel exports"] after a brief halt during its Golden Week holiday, also weighed on the market. Reuters reported the development on Friday, citing sources. On a weekly basis, Brent and WTI prices are set to rise. Trump's Iran pledge along with China's resumption of product exports were moving prices lower, said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga. Prices have been volatile this week as threats to shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20% of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased. On Thursday, Trump said Washington was having "productive discussions" with Iran and said [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"no attack"] was planned before the November 3 midterm congressional elections after media reports that he was considering an attack before then. Iran's Tasnim news agency reported the same day that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran is reviewing the US response to its proposal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. The US is still pressuring Iran economically, imposing sanctions targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals. The Iran war and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have disrupted supplies of refined fuels such as gasoline, jet fuel and especially diesel fuel. The oil market is also contending with [USN:L1N45U0RS TEXT:"Hurricane Isaias"] in the Gulf of Mexico where producers have shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or 62.9%, of current oil production as of Thursday, according to the US Marine Minerals Administration.

item.title: Gold hits one-week high, heads for weekly gain on bargain-hunting
item.description: Gold rose for a second straight session on Friday, touching a one-week high, as bargain buying emerged after bullion fell to two-month low earlier this week, while traders assessed the likelihood of further US Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sinha
item.content:encoded: Gold rose for a second straight session on Friday, touching a one-week high, as bargain buying emerged after bullion fell to two-month low earlier this week, while traders assessed the likelihood of further US Federal Reserve interest rate hikes. Spot gold rose 1.5% to $4,194.36 per ounce by 03:29 p.m. EDT (1929 GMT), heading for a weekly gain of about 1.3%. The metal fell to a two-month low on Wednesday as a stronger dollar and rising US Treasury yields weighed on the non-yielding metal. US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.4% to settle at $4,216.3. Bullion gained due to "bargain hunting at the lows, as a floor has been building in the $4,000-region," said Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis at Stone X. "It is arguable that a further Fed hike is already priced in but so is the expectation for continued official sector net purchases. Without any Black Swan event I find it hard to see gold breaking convincingly higher." US 10-year Treasury yields were off over two-decade highs hit on Wednesday. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said on Thursday the US central bank [USN:L6N45U16W TEXT:"will need to hike rates again to bring inflation back to its 2% target"]. Traders are pricing in a 19% chance of a rate hike in October and an 84% probability of at least one 25-basis-point increase by December, according to the CME's FedWatch tool. Gold tends to lose its appeal compared to yield-bearing assets in a high interest-rate environment. "The coming week's CPI release may act as a catalyst for gold's next big move... Still-stubborn inflation that pushes the Fed into a steeper rate-hike cycle may force spot gold to re-test the psychological $4,000 support once more," said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit. Meanwhile, [USN:L4N45V08X TEXT:"gold demand in India"] was sluggish this week as prices rebounded, while trading in top consumer China was subdued during the holiday-truncated trading period. Among other metals, spot silver gained 2.4% to $60.77 per ounce. Platinum jumped 3.1% to $1,685.64 and palladium rose 2.1% to $1,146.39. Both metals were headed for weekly losses.

item.title: Euro falls, set for fifth straight weekly drop as oil prices rise
item.description: The euro was poised for a fifth straight weekly drop on Friday, with early gains fading as oil prices erased earlier declines, but recent selling pressure was muted as France's beleaguered bond market steadied.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak
item.content:encoded: The euro was poised for a fifth straight weekly drop on Friday, with early gains fading as oil prices erased earlier declines, but recent selling pressure was muted as France's beleaguered bond market steadied. The euro zone's currency hit a 17-month low of $1.1161 on Monday as investors worried about France's record public debt and the difficult political path to budget cuts, in contrast with a robust-looking US economy and currency. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.13% to 102.25. The index was up about 0.3% on the week and on track for a fourth straight weekly gain, its longest run since May 2025. The euro was last down 0.1% at $1.1198, and off about 0.5% on the week as it was poised for its longest streak of weekly declines against the dollar since the start of 2025. Risk premiums on French and Italian government debt [USN:L1N45V0AF TEXT:"were on track"] for a weekly decline after jumping in late September, as investors looked for fresh developments before demanding higher compensation for fiscal and political risks. TRUMP SIGNALS NO IRAN ATTACK Global bond markets had calmed earlier on Friday as [USN:L1N45V03A TEXT:"oil prices fell"] after US President Donald Trump said that the US would not attack Iran before US midterm elections on November 3 and added that there had been productive talks with Tehran over the war. "As it stands right now, you have a confluence of factors — you have higher oil prices, you have the issue in France, so it is really tough to say what is moving the market more than the other," said Eugene Epstein, head of trading and structured products at Moneycorp in Stamford, Connecticut. "But practically speaking, I'd say today is in a relative holding pattern, everyone is just waiting for all the Fed speak to make its way through, because certainly you can see that the sensitivity of the dollar is high to the entire range of Fed speakers now," Epstein said. Crude prices moved off their lows, however, as British navy-affiliated agency [USN:L1N45V0GU TEXT:"UKMTO said"] a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the United Arab Emirates. US crude rose 0.6% to $92.04 a barrel after falling as low as $90.01 and Brent advanced to $104.88 per barrel, up 0.58% on the day, after declining to $102.33. Bond yields around the world have climbed in recent weeks due to expectations of central bank rate hikes as well as concerns about government finances. CENTRAL BANK POLICY IN FOCUS But expectations for a rate hike from the Fed at its policy meeting later this month remain subdued, with markets pricing in a 19.4% chance for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points, according to CME FedWatch , even as recent economic data has pointed to persistent inflation pressure. However, investors are pricing in an 85.8% chance for a hike at the central bank's December meeting. On Friday, the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers showed US [USN:L1N45V0J1 TEXT:"consumer sentiment slumped further"] in early October as the rising cost of living because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy. While many Fed officials have indicated more rate hikes will be needed to curb inflation, others have pushed back on the need for immediate hikes, and suggested the Fed should be patient and flexible in deciding the rate path. French debt has been under pressure as politicians struggle to curb the budget deficit ahead of a divisive election in 2027. The calling of a snap election in Spain earlier in the week also added to the pressure on the euro. Sterling gained 0.08% to $1.3235 but was on track for a seventh straight week of declines, its longest stretch since November 2024. Against the yen , the dollar strengthened 0.25% to 158.25. The Japanese currency was on pace for its fourth straight weekly decline against the greenback, down about 0.2% on the week.

item.title: New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
item.description: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses.
item.dc:creator: Julia Harte, Kristina Cooke
item.content:encoded: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses. Federal immigration agents have shot at least 21 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, [USN:L1N43J0KR TEXT:"7 fatally"], sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Trump's push to [USN:L6N4510WH TEXT:"ramp up deportations"] has led to an [USN:L6N3YA11U TEXT:"increasing number of violent confrontations"], and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved. Trump has said many migrants must be deported, blaming them, often in sweeping terms, for financial fraud and violent crimes. "Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "I have been on the phone with President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary Mullin, negotiating the release of the man ICE agents shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful," Mamdani said in a press conference late in the evening. He said he demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. "These actions are making the city less safe," Mamdani said. "This city wants ICE out. We want ICE out of our city, ICE out of our schools, ICE out of our hospitals, ICE out of our streets, ICE away from our kids." The mayor said the child in the car is physically unharmed. New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said NYPD has located the child with a family member after a wellness check. The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement ICE officers were conducting a "targeted enforcement operation" in the Bronx, New York, to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction. The man identified as 28-year-old, had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025, according to NYPD Commissioner Tisch. "During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured," DHS said, adding that ICE officers rendered immediate aid. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital." The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. ET (2000 GMT), DHS said. Working at a restaurant near the shooting, Pedro Almarez said he heard shots fired and went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at the scene. "There were a lot of ICE officers, three or four cars," Almarez told Reuters by phone. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later. He said the man was only removed from his car after an ambulance arrived. At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on a balcony overlooking the area told officers they were "taking our children," according to a Reuters witness.

item.title: US to livestream Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
item.description: The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution.
item.dc:creator: Phil Stewart
item.content:encoded: The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by [USN:L1N45S037 TEXT:"firing squad"] by the US military since 1945. The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the [USN:L1N45M04O TEXT:"botched lethal injection"] of a Tennessee woman last week. "It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post. Media have sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, experts said. Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging of a young Black man who had been convicted of raping a white woman. Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 p.m. — the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting — was a "no-brainer." "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public. Because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3." PRESIDENT MUST APPROVE FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder. The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest. Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. [USN:L1N45T015 TEXT:"President Donald Trump did so"] on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday. The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon. The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the center reported. "It would be extremely, extremely strange" to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School. While firing squads have a long history in American military law, as far as he knew it would be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death. "The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it's an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, 'Well, it was OK in 1790, so what the hell?'" Fidell said. Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public. "What's the point of it? Who would want to see that?" said Lurie. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, [USN:L2N3PP0X8 TEXT:"South Carolina"] carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years. Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration[USN:L6N417125 TEXT:" recently added"] to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized. Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke "[USN:L1N45T0M9 TEXT:"angry and confused"]" in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

item.title: The tech green-card program under attack from Trump
item.description: The US government said on Thursday it is suspending some major global tech and IT firms including Microsoft and Cognizant from a key green card program that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia, Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: The US government said on Thursday it is [USN:L6N45U111 TEXT:"suspending"] some major global tech and IT firms including Microsoft and Cognizant from a key green card program that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment. Senior US officials cited alleged fraud as the reason behind the move, saying companies have been using the program to replace American workers with cheaper foreign workers, and comes as the latest step in the Trump administration's crackdown on skilled foreign labor. WHAT IS UNDER SUSPENSION? The suspension is targeting a key employer-sponsorship mechanism, called the Permanent Labor Certification or PERM, which is used by major technology companies and outsourcing firms. The US government said that for certain companies, it would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones. PERM came into effect in 2005, aiming to speed up the long processing times experienced under the previous paper-based "Alien Employment Certification" program. Under PERM, the US Department of Labor (DOL) allows an employer to sponsor a foreign worker's permanent residency. The process is initiated by qualified US employers, and not individual workers. The Labor Department must certify to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services that there are not enough US workers that are qualified and available for a given job opportunity, and that the employment of the foreign worker will not affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans. Outside of PERM and family-based routes to permanent residency, individuals can also self-petition for green cards through processes such as the EB-1A application for individuals with extraordinary ability or the EB-2 National Interest Waiver. WHY IS IT IMPORTANT? The PERM program serves as a critical bridge between temporary work status and a green card for many foreign skilled workers. Many IT firms employ hundreds of thousands of workers who typically start on temporary work visas such as the H-1B, and later seek permanent residency. Without the option to be sponsored by their employer under PERM, foreign workers could lose a key route to permanent residency and would have to stay on temporary visas for longer. For companies, recruiting foreign talent could become harder, as many workers overseas view the path to permanent US residency as a key reason for taking a job. WHICH COMPANIES ARE UNDER SUSPENSION? The US said it is suspending Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Adobe (ADBE.O) along with some of the largest IT firms in the world, including Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . Other companies such as Meta (META.O) , Amazon (AMZN.O) or Alphabet's Google (GOOGL.O) remain free to participate in the program. WHY IS THE US FREEZING APPLICATIONS? The move widens an ongoing crackdown on visas for foreign workers, which the Trump administration has said cost US jobs. Vice President JD Vance said, without citing specific evidence, companies are using the PERM program to replace American employees with foreign workers and undercut their wages. Vance said on Thursday: "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers." The suspensions follow President Trump's move to impose a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, which has been blocked by federal court orders. HOW IS PERM DIFFERENT FROM H-1B? H-1B is a temporary work visa that allows skilled foreign workers to work in the US, generally for up to six years. PERM, meanwhile, is a permanent labor-certification process. The freeze does not appear to directly affect current holders of H-1B visas. HOW CURTAILING PERM COULD BACKFIRE Some experts said that while the PERM suspensions might target specific companies, such policies risk making the US less competitive globally by deterring highly skilled foreign talent. "It is a fallacy to think that you can protect American workers by keeping skilled foreign workers out of the country. You think that foreign talent competes with Americans within our borders, they'll certainly compete with Americans by working abroad," said Chad Sparber, Director of the Lampert Institute for Civic and Global Affairs at Colgate University. Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Immigration Policy Lab, said that permanent residency is the primary way for talented foreign workers to stay in the country and without it, some will leave, and some will not come in the first place, even temporarily.

item.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens as US Gulf Coast prepares for landfall
item.description: Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding.
item.dc:creator: Brad Brooks
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding. Isaias has already severely disrupted oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico, forcing energy companies to evacuate offshore platforms and shut down operations. The first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season was packing maximum sustained winds of 85 mph (140 kph) early on Thursday, the US National Hurricane Center said. Isaias was forecast to strengthen to near Category 3 intensity, with sustained winds reaching 110 mph (175 kph) on Friday before reaching the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday. "We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” NHC director Michael Brennan said in a Thursday morning briefing. "Today is the day to prepare and get ready." Isaias nearly tied the record for the latest first Atlantic hurricane with one that hit on October 8, 1905. The strong El Nino weather pattern this year has suppressed Atlantic hurricane development by increasing vertical wind shear, which disrupts the formation of strengthening tropical storms. The hurricane was moving east-northeast at 10 mph (17 kph), about 355 miles (570 km) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River at 1 p.m. US Central time, the NHC said. IMPACTS ON OIL, GAS The Marine Minerals Administration, which monitors offshore US oil and gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico, said on Thursday that personnel have been evacuated from 121 production platforms and five non-dynamically positioned rigs ahead of the storm. About 63% of current oil production in the Gulf, or 1.3 million barrels of oil a day, has been shut in, the agency said, citing operator reports. Just over 1.1 billion cubic feet a day of natural gas production has also been shut in, or about 57% of total output from the region. On Wednesday, 25% of oil production and 16% of natural gas output had been shut in. About 9 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates. The companies with the most exposure to the storm include BP, Chevron (CVX.N) , ENI, Murphy Oil (MUR.N) and Shell (SHEL.L) , among others, according to the Earth Science model. WARNINGS, STORM SURGE Hurricane warnings stretched from coastal Mississippi through Alabama to the Florida panhandle, while tropical-storm and storm-surge warnings extended into southeastern Louisiana, the NHC said. Forecasters warned that storm surges could reach 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2.1 meters) above sea level in the hardest-hit coastal areas, with rainfall of 3 to 7 inches (8 to 18 cm) and isolated totals of 15 inches (38 cm). The hurricane was forecast to weaken somewhat as it approached land. Increasing vertical wind shear, which can disrupt a hurricane's circulation, was expected to limit its strength near landfall, though forecasters warned it would remain dangerous. EVACUATIONS ORDERED In Florida, officials ordered mandatory evacuations beginning at noon local time on Thursday for coastal areas of Okaloosa County. The county urged tourists to leave the area and announced plans to close three airports Thursday evening. Governor Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in 25 Florida counties earlier in the week. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency covering 40 counties, while officials on Dauphin Island issued an evacuation notice for the western portion of the barrier island beginning Thursday evening. Baldwin County, Alabama, encouraged residents of low-lying coastal areas to evacuate voluntarily and prepared emergency shelters. In Mississippi, Jackson County and the city of Gautier declared local emergencies as coastal communities prepared for flooding and power outages.

item.title: South Africa blames disinformation as anti-migrant protests turn violent
item.description: Anti-migrant protests in two South African cities including Johannesburg's Soweto township turned violent on Thursday, with the government blaming disinformation over a court ruling on asylum seekers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anti-migrant protests in two South African cities including Johannesburg's Soweto township turned violent on Thursday, with the government blaming disinformation over a court ruling on asylum seekers. In coastal Durban, the second city hit by protests, a Reuters reporter saw five torched cars in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted. The unrest followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee centre stop processing asylum applications. In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop that they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. The looters fled after police arrived and made them disperse. Government spokesperson William Baloyi said the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about a constitutional court ruling in July. The country's highest court ruled that asylum seekers cannot be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely for procedural reasons such as having entered the country illegally. Baloyi said the ruling had been widely misrepresented and did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants. "We are deeply concerned by what is going on now," he added. Police said in a statement that they had mobilised more officers in Durban, where they said at least 14 vehicles had been set alight while a guest house and warehouse were partially burned. A top police official, Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane, told a press conference in Soweto: "Those responsible for acts of violence and destruction will be identified, investigated and where sufficient evidence exists, arrested and brought to book." Dimpane said 10 vehicles had been burned in Soweto but the situation was now under control. South Africa has seen months of [USN:L1N43205U TEXT:"anti-migrant marches"] this year that have drawn international criticism. Some of the marches have descended into violence and looting, and thousands of African foreign nationals have fled the country. Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, claims that social scientists say are not supported by evidence. Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Despite this, it remains Africa's largest economy and continues to draw migrants.
